Procure
pro-cure'
v.t. (to obtain; to bring about; to cause to come to one)
Latin procurare, to take care of, manage, from pro- and curare, to care for, from cura, care. To procure is to bring a thing about by taking pains over it.

Biblical Definition

Jeremiah has the word twice, and the two uses are the two directions a man's pains can run. The elders of the land defend Jeremiah by recalling Micah's case under Hezekiah, and conclude: “Thus might we procure great evil against our souls” (Jer 26:19). Killing the prophet would not merely be wrong; it would be a thing the killers brought upon themselves — procured, obtained, worked for. Sin in Scripture is frequently described this way, as a purchase a man makes with his own hands and then has to keep. The second use has God as the one taking pains: Jerusalem restored “shall be to me a name of joy, a praise and an honour before all the nations of the earth, which shall hear all the good that I do unto them: and they shall fear and tremble for all the goodness and for all the prosperity that I procure unto it” (Jer 33:9). God procures prosperity for a city He had just given over to the Chaldeans, and the nations tremble — not at the judgment, but at the goodness. Solomon states the general rule both ways: “He that diligently seeketh good procureth favour: but he that seeketh mischief, it shall come unto him” (Pro 11:27).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines procure as to get; to gain; to obtain, as by request, loan, effort, labor or purchase; to persuade or prevail on; and to cause; to bring on; to draw to.

expand to see more

PROCU'RE, v.t. [L. procuro; pro and curo, to take care.]

1. To get; to gain; to obtain; as by request, loan, effort, labor or purchase.

We procure favor by kindness.

2. To persuade; to prevail on.

3. To cause; to bring on; to draw to; to attract. Thus might we procure great evil against our souls. Jer. 26.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 33:9 — "And it shall be to me a name of joy, a praise and an honour before all the nations of the earth, which shall hear all the good that I do unto them: and they shall fear and tremble for all the goodness and for all the prosperity that I procure unto it."

Jeremiah 26:19 — "Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him at all to death? did he not fear the LORD, and besought the LORD, and the LORD repented him of the evil which he had pronounced against them? Thus might we procure great evil against our souls."

Proverbs 11:27 — "He that diligently seeketh good procureth favour: but he that seeketh mischief, it shall come unto him."

Galatians 6:7 — "Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap."

Modern Corruption

The prosperity gospel has made procuring God's goodness a technique, while Jeremiah has God procuring it for a city that had earned the opposite.

expand to see more

Proverbs 11:27 is the sort of verse the prosperity teachers build on — seek good and you shall procure favour — read as a mechanism a believer can operate. Proverbs states general wisdom, not a formula with a guarantee attached, and the same book that promises favour to the diligent also observes that the race is not always to the swift. More decisively, Jeremiah 33:9 puts God in the subject position: the prosperity that I procure unto it. The city could not procure it. The city had procured exile. When restoration comes, the nations tremble at goodness precisely because nobody can account for it on the basis of desert.

The opposite error is a fatalism that hears Jeremiah 33:9 and concludes that human pains are irrelevant, which Jeremiah 26:19 immediately blocks. The elders argue that killing a prophet would procure great evil against our souls — a real consequence, really brought about by a real choice, and their argument saved Jeremiah's life that day. Scripture holds both without strain: God procures what He gives, and men procure what they sow (Gal 6:7). A theology that drops either half produces either a magician or a spectator.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew asah (H6213), to do, make, bring about; biqqesh (H1245), to seek diligently; Latin procurare, to take care of.

expand to see more

Hebrew oseh lah (H6213) — that I do for it; Jeremiah 33:9, the prosperity God Himself brings about.

Hebrew osim ra'ah gedolah al naphshotenu — doing great evil against our souls; Jeremiah 26:19, sin as a thing worked for.

Hebrew shocher tob (H7836) — seeking good early and diligently; Proverbs 11:27.

Hebrew ratson (H7522) — favour, good pleasure; what the diligent seeker procures.

Latin procurare, from cura — care; Webster's root, to bring about by taking pains.

Usage

"“The prosperity that I procure unto it” — God in the subject position."

"“Thus might we procure great evil against our souls” — sin as a purchase."

"“He that diligently seeketh good procureth favour” — wisdom, not machinery."
